LO 1Mitochondrial physiology

Q1. What are mitochondria, and what do they do?
  • Intracellular organelle; 100s–1000s per cell, in every cell except mature RBCs (RBCs run on glycolysis)
  • Maternally inherited; have their own genome
  • Main job = metabolism: ATP by oxidative phosphorylation; hub of most metabolic pathways; also regulate apoptosis
Analogy — the power-plant blackout

Mitochondria are the city's power plants. In a blackout, the biggest power customers fail first: brain, muscle, heart, retina, ear, kidney tubules, liver, gut. That's why the disease looks like "anything."

Q2. What is primary vs secondary mitochondrial dysfunction?

Primary

  • Genetic defect in a critical mitochondrial protein
  • Gene can be in the nuclear OR mitochondrial genome

Secondary

  • Infections
  • Medications
  • Other physiologic stressors (fever, fasting, surgery)
Step 1 — drugs that hurt mitochondria
  • Valproate: inhibits respiratory chain; fatal liver failure in POLG/Alpers
  • Barbiturates: inhibit complex I
  • Aminoglycosides: deafness with 12S rRNA m.1555A>G
  • NRTIs (zidovudine), linezolid: myopathy, lactic acidosis
Q3. What clinical features can mitochondrial disease cause?

"Anything, anywhere, anytime." Don't memorize the list; understand why each energy-hungry tissue fails.

SystemFeatures
SystemicLactic acidosis, short stature, fatigue, failure to gain weight
CNSMyoclonus, generalized seizures, stroke, migraine, ataxia, intellectual disability, psychiatric disease
MuscleMyopathy (hypotonia), CPEO, recurrent myoglobinuria, weakness/fatigue
HeartCardiomyopathy, conduction defects
EyeOptic neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa
EarHigh-frequency hearing loss, aminoglycoside-induced deafness
GIPseudo-obstruction, constipation, vomiting
LiverHypoglycemia, gluconeogenic defects, liver failure, cirrhosis
KidneyFanconi syndrome (proximal tubule)
EndocrineDiabetes insipidus, hormonal dysfunction
Bone marrowAnemia, pancytopenia
High yield

Red flags: ≥3 unrelated organ systems (brain + muscle especially), worsening with illness or fasting, lactic acidosis, maternal family history.

Step 1

Lactate:pyruvate ratio: ETC defect → NADH piles up → pyruvate pushed to lactate → high L:P (>20). PDH deficiency → both rise together → normal L:P. Muscle biopsy: ragged red fibers (Gomori trichrome). Classic triad: deafness + diabetes mellitus + short stature.

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1Which cell type has no mitochondria, and how does it make ATP?
Mature RBCs: glycolysis only.
A2Why does almost any mitochondrial defect raise blood lactate?
A block in the TCA/ETC backs up NADH and pyruvate; pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis.

LO 2Mitochondrial genetics

Q1. What is unique about mitochondrial DNA?
FeaturemtDNA
Size / shape≈16.5 kb, double-stranded, circular
Genes37: 22 tRNAs (distinct triplet code from nuclear DNA) · 2 rRNAs · 13 ETC subunits
Copies2–10 per mitochondrion → thousands per cell
Nuclear shareMost of the >1,000 mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded

Human mtDNA map

  • 16,569 bp circle; tRNAs (yellow) scattered between protein genes
Memory tool

37 = 22 + 2 + 13: "22 tRNAs carry, 2 rRNAs build, 13 proteins burn." tRNA genes are the classic disease sites (MELAS tRNA-Leu, MERRF tRNA-Lys).

Step 1

Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is the only ETC complex with no mtDNA-encoded subunits.

Q2. What does a maternal-inheritance pedigree look like?
Parent with an mtDNA mutationChildren
MotherAll children inherit it (sons and daughters), with variable severity
FatherNone (sperm mitochondria are lost after fertilization)

Maternal transmission

  • mtDNA marker passes only through mothers
High yield

Passed only through females, both sexes affected, affected men never transmit, severity varies within a sibship → mitochondrial. Contrast XLR (affected father → all daughters carriers) and AD (male-to-male transmission possible).

Q3. What are homoplasmy, heteroplasmy, threshold and bottleneck?
TermMeaning
HomoplasmyAll mtDNA copies in a cell are the same (all normal or all mutant)
HeteroplasmyA mix of normal and mutant mtDNA in a cell or tissue
ThresholdSymptoms only when the mutant fraction passes a tissue-specific level (30% mutant → none? 70% → symptoms?)
Tissue variationHeteroplasmy differs tissue to tissue and shifts with cell division
BottleneckOnly a small, random sample of mom's mitochondria enters each egg → a mildly affected mother can have a severely affected child

Homoplasmy vs heteroplasmy

  • 30% mutant = no symptoms? 70% = symptoms?

Bottleneck

  • Eggs get 80%, 50% or 20% mutant → severe, mild, none
High yield

Variable severity of the same mtDNA mutation within one family = heteroplasmy (not anticipation, imprinting or locus heterogeneity).

Analogy — the bag of marbles

Mom's egg precursor holds a bag of red (mutant) and green (normal) marbles. Each egg grabs a small random handful. One child gets mostly red, a sibling mostly green.

Trap — counseling

A woman with a heteroplasmic mtDNA point mutation passes it to all offspring, but CVS/amniocentesis can't reliably predict severity: heteroplasmy shifts during development and differs between tissues.

Q4. Can mitochondrial disease be inherited any other way?
  • Yes: because most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded, disease can be maternal, X-linked, autosomal recessive (most common!) or autosomal dominant
  • Affected siblings with healthy parents and a mitochondrial phenotype → think AR nuclear
In-house exam

Autosomal recessive nuclear genes are the most common cause of mitochondrial disease.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A man and a woman each have LHON. What is the risk to each one's children?
Man: none (fathers don't transmit mtDNA). Woman: all children inherit the mutation; clinical risk varies (heteroplasmy, incomplete penetrance).
A2A patient has mild cramps; his maternal aunt has deafness and CPEO; biopsy shows a variable % of mutant mtDNA across fibers. Principle?
Heteroplasmy.

LO 3Representative disorders

Q1. MELAS: who gets it, and what are "ATP strokes"?

Mitochondrial Encephalopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes.

Clinical

  • Childhood onset
  • First: non-specific neuro symptoms: seizures, headaches, altered consciousness, transient hemiparesis or blindness
  • Then progressive motor, visual and cognitive decline
  • Lactic acidosis; myopathy
  • Stroke-like episodes = "ATP strokes, not clot strokes"

Genetics & treatment

  • mtDNA: 80% in MT-TL1 (tRNA-Leu); common mutation m.3243A>G
  • Maternal inheritance; heteroplasmy and tissue distribution shape the phenotype
  • "Cocktail": CoQ10, carnitine, creatine, lipoic acid (supportive)
  • Arginine during acute stroke-like events
In-house exam

3-year-old with a seizure after 3 days of fever, months of regression, ↑ lactate in blood and CSF, an occipital cortical lesion → MELAS, maternal inheritance.

High yield — MELAS vs ischemic stroke

Young patient, no vascular risk factors, lesion crosses arterial territories (often occipital), lactate high, triggered by illness, maternal relatives with varied symptoms → metabolic "ATP stroke."

Memory tool

Why arginine? Arginine → nitric oxide → vasodilation → more blood and nutrients to the stressed brain. The cocktail = cofactors that "support a stressed mitochondrion," not a cure.

Q2. PDH deficiency: why X-linked, and why a ketogenic diet?
  • PDH links glycolysis to the TCA cycle (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA); a multi-enzyme complex
  • Cofactors: thiamine, α-lipoic acid, FAD, NAD, CoA
  • Gene PDHA1 is X-linked, but males and females can be affected (skewed X-inactivation in brain); complete loss is fatal early in both
  • Clinical: psychomotor delay, hypotonia, progressive encephalopathy (incl. Leigh) with early death, brain malformations; occasional cardiomyopathy, liver
  • Treatment: ketogenic diet (ketones → acetyl-CoA after the block = alternate brain fuel); cofactors help only if some enzyme activity remains

PDH = the gateway

  • Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → TCA

PDH deficiency MRI

  • Brain malformations / breakdown
Memory tool

PDH cofactors: "Tender Loving Care For Nancy" = Thiamine (B1), Lipoic acid, CoA (B5), FAD (B2), NAD (B3). Same five as α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

Trap

X-linked ≠ "boys only": the slide says male and female can be affected. And carbohydrate loads worsen lactic acidosis in PDH deficiency.

Step 1

PDH deficiency → ↑ lactate and pyruvate (normal L:P ratio), ↑ alanine. Arsenic inhibits lipoic acid.

Q3. MNGIE: how does a nuclear gene damage mtDNA?

Mitochondrial NeuroGastroIntestinal Encephalopathy.

  • Onset in adolescence (variable)
  • Severe GI dysmotility, cachexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, incontinence; peripheral neuropathy; ophthalmoplegia/ptosis
  • Cause: thymidine phosphorylase deficiency (TYMP), a nuclear-encoded, cytoplasmic protein → autosomal recessive
  • Massive ↑ thymidine → disrupts mtDNA replication (which needs tight nucleotide control) → progressive accumulation of mtDNA mutations
Memory tool

MNGIE = "My Nerves, Gut, Intestines, Eyes": neuropathy, gut dysmotility, cachexia, ptosis/ophthalmoplegia.

Analogy — the flooded supply room

mtDNA replication is a printer that needs exactly the right ink mix. Thymidine phosphorylase deficiency floods the room with one color (thymidine) and the copies come out full of errors.

Q4. Leigh syndrome: what is it, and why do so many genes cause it?
  • Progressive neurologic degeneration starting at 3–12 months
  • Decompensation with each catabolic stress (infection, fasting)
  • Hypotonia, spasticity, chorea, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy; cardiomyopathy
  • Brainstem and/or basal ganglia disease; ↑ lactate in blood or CSF (MRS lactate peak)
  • Genetic heterogeneity: many genes → one disease ("the brain showing us the mitochondria aren't working")
ComplexmtDNA-encodedNuclear-encoded
IMTND3, MTND5, MTND6NDUFV1, NDUFS1, S3, S4, S7, S8
II—SDHA (flavoprotein subunit A)
III—BCS1L (assembly)
IVMTCO3COX10, COX15, SCO2, SURF1 (assembly of complex IV)
VMTATP6—
Other—PDH (X-linked)

Leigh imaging

  • Basal ganglia lesions (top); MRS lactate peak (bottom)

Management: no specific treatment · sodium bicarbonate for acidosis · antiepileptics but avoid valproic acid and barbiturates (inhibit the respiratory chain) · mitochondrial cocktail trial · hospice care.

In-house exam

7-month-old regresses after a viral illness; MRI symmetric basal ganglia/brainstem lesions; CSF lactate ↑ → Leigh. Avoid valproate and barbiturates.

Memory tool

Leigh = "Lots of genes, Lactate, Little ones, Lentiform (basal ganglia)."

Q5. POLG1: how does one gene cause many diseases?
  • POLG1 = mtDNA polymerase γ, critical for mtDNA replication and repair; 3 domains (polymerase, exonuclease, linker) with some genotype–phenotype correlation
  • Continuum of overlapping phenotypes varying in severity, organ and age of onset; all originally described separately
  • Diagnosed by direct mutation detection or mtDNA depletion; no specific effective therapy
  • Phenotypic heterogeneity: one gene → many diseases
PhenotypeFeatures
Leigh diseaseCNS imaging findings; rapid deterioration in childhood
AlpersSeizures, neurologic regression, liver dysfunction or failure
MEMSAMyoclonic epilepsy, myopathy, sensory ataxia
ANSAtaxia neuropathy spectrum
AR and AD PEOProgressive external ophthalmoplegia (adults)
In-house exam

Leigh = genetic heterogeneity (many genes → one disease). POLG1 = phenotypic heterogeneity (one gene → many diseases). Easy to flip on the exam.

High yield

Valproate + POLG = acute liver failure. Children with refractory seizures and regression are tested for POLG1 before mitochondria-toxic antiepileptics.

Q6. Which classic mitochondrial syndromes does Step 1 add?
SyndromeGeneticsHallmarks
MERRFmtDNA tRNA-Lys (m.8344A>G), maternalMyoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers; ataxia, myopathy, hearing loss
LHONmtDNA complex I (ND4), maternalYoung men; acute painless bilateral central vision loss
Kearns-SayreSingle large mtDNA deletion, sporadicOnset <20: CPEO + pigmentary retinopathy + heart block
PearsonLarge mtDNA deletion, sporadicInfants: sideroblastic anemia + exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; can evolve to KSS
Aminoglycoside deafness12S rRNA m.1555A>GIrreversible deafness after one course
Step 1 — sorters
  • Ragged red trio: MERRF, MELAS, Kearns-Sayre
  • Ophthalmoplegia: KSS (+ retinopathy + heart block, <20) · POLG PEO (adult) · MNGIE (+ GI + neuropathy)
  • Vision: LHON = optic neuropathy · KSS/MERRF = retinopathy · MELAS = cortical blindness

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A 2-month-old girl has hypotonia and corpus callosum agenesis; lactate and pyruvate are both ↑ with a normal L:P ratio. Enzyme, inheritance and diet?
PDH (PDHA1), X-linked (girls can be affected), ketogenic diet.
A2A 19-year-old has pseudo-obstruction, 20 kg weight loss, ptosis and neuropathy; plasma thymidine is very high. Diagnosis and inheritance?
MNGIE: TYMP (thymidine phosphorylase), autosomal recessive.
A3A child with refractory seizures and regression develops liver failure after starting valproate. Gene?
POLG1 → Alpers.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A 3-year-old has a tonic-clonic seizure after 3 days of fever and 3 months of motor regression. Lactate is ↑ in blood and CSF; MRI shows a left occipital cortical lesion that doesn't fit a vascular territory. Inheritance pattern?

MELAS: m.3243A>G in MT-TL1, maternal inheritance.

2Which gene type carries most MELAS mutations?

80% in MT-TL1 (tRNA-Leu), usually m.3243A>G.

3During an acute stroke-like episode in MELAS, which therapy is given?

Arginine → NO → vasodilation → more blood to the stressed brain. These are ATP strokes, not clots.

4A woman has a heteroplasmic mtDNA point mutation and mild symptoms. Which statement about her children is correct?

Maternal transmission to all; bottleneck and tissue variation make severity unpredictable.

5Affected family members carry the same mtDNA mutation but range from mild cramps to severe encephalopathy. Best explanation?

Different mutant loads per person and tissue = heteroplasmy.

6What is the most common inheritance pattern of mitochondrial disease?

Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded → AR is most common.

7An infant girl has hypotonia, brain malformations, and ↑ lactate and pyruvate with a normal L:P ratio. Which treatment is most effective?

PDH deficiency: ketones bypass the block; carbohydrates worsen lactic acidosis.

8A 17-year-old has severe GI dysmotility, cachexia, ptosis and peripheral neuropathy. Plasma thymidine is markedly elevated. Defective protein?

MNGIE: TYMP, nuclear, AR → thymidine excess damages mtDNA.

9A 7-month-old regresses after each viral illness. MRI shows symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions; CSF lactate is ↑. Which antiseizure drug should be avoided?

Leigh syndrome: avoid valproate and barbiturates (inhibit the respiratory chain).

10Leigh syndrome can result from mutations in complex I, II, III, IV, V or PDH genes. This illustrates:

Many genes → one disease = genetic heterogeneity. POLG1 is the opposite.

11A child with refractory seizures and developmental regression develops acute liver failure after starting valproate. Most likely gene?

POLG1 / Alpers: seizures, regression, liver failure; valproate precipitates it.

12How many genes does human mtDNA encode, and which group is largest?

37 = 22 tRNAs + 2 rRNAs + 13 ETC subunits.
